title: How apps talk: requests, status codes and JSON

say: How apps talk: requests, status codes, and JSON.
This is the video for module one of API Fundamentals.
An API, short for Application Programming Interface, is a published set of rules that lets one program ask another for data or an action.
The client is the program that asks, like a phone app. The server is the computer that answers.

panel.heading: An API is a published set of rules
items: The client asks, the server answers
The question is a request
The answer is a response
You will read both, with no code

say: The question is called a request, and the answer is a response. Most web APIs use HTTPS, the same secure language your browser uses.

say: Think of a buka. You order from the menu, the attendant takes it to the kitchen, and food comes back. The menu is the documentation, the attendant is the API, and you never see the kitchen.

say: Each thing you can ask for has its own address, called an endpoint. Take a request to Open-Meteo, a free weather API. The scheme, https, means the conversation is encrypted.

panel.heading: The parts of an API URL
items: Scheme: https, an encrypted conversation
Host: the server you are talking to
Path: which endpoint, such as /v1/forecast
Query string: settings after the question mark

say: Next is the host, api.open-meteo.com, the server you are talking to.

say: Every request has a method, the verb. GET fetches a copy. PUT replaces a whole item, PATCH changes some fields, and DELETE removes one.
GET is safe: it only reads, so it cannot harm anything.

panel.heading: Safe to repeat, or not?
left: Fine to test in a browser

say: POST sends new data, such as starting a payment. It is not safe to repeat. If a POST seems to hang, do not press send again. You could create two payments. First check, using the transaction reference, whether the first one went through.

panel.heading: Safe to repeat, or not?
left: Fine to test in a browser

say: Every response has a status code, a three-digit number saying how it went. A 2 at the start means success.

cards.d: 200 OK. 201 Created, common after POST. 204 No Content, common after DELETE.
401: prove who you are. 403: known but not allowed. 404 Not Found. 429 Too Many Requests.
500, 502, 503. Wait, check the provider's status page, retry only safe requests.

say: A 4 means the problem is in your request. A 401 means check that your key is present and typed correctly. A 403 means the server knows you, but you need different permissions.
For example, Funmi traced a 400 error to a latitude typed with a comma instead of a full stop.

say: A 5 means the problem is on their side. Wait, check their status page, and retry only safe requests.

say: JSON is plain text with strict rules. An object sits in curly brackets and holds keys and values, like an email address with its label.

panel.heading: Boxes inside boxes
items: Object: curly brackets, keys and values
Array: square brackets, an ordered list
Data path: dots for keys, numbers for items
Arrays count from 0, not 1

say: An array sits in square brackets and holds a list in order.

say: A data path gives directions to one value. For Paystack's sample response, data dot reference points to the code you use later to check the payment.

items: Object: curly brackets, keys and values

say: Arrays count from 0. So index 0 is the first item, and asking for index 1 gives the second. Halima in Abuja read four hourly temperatures, index 0 to 3, and averaged them to 28.3 degrees Celsius.

say: Payment APIs usually avoid decimal points by sending money in the smallest unit. Paystack's documentation says naira amounts are sent in kobo.

panel.heading: The kobo rule
items: Payment APIs send money in subunits
For naira, that is kobo
Divide kobo by 100 to read naira
1500000 kobo is 15,000 naira

say: So divide by 100 to read. An amount of 1,500,000 kobo is 15,000 naira.

panel.heading: The kobo rule
items: Payment APIs send money in subunits
For naira, that is kobo
Divide kobo by 100 to read naira
1500000 kobo is 15,000 naira

say: Forget this, and a 15,000 naira payment looks like 1.5 million in a report. Also, a number in quotes is text, and null means unknown, not zero.
Never paste a response with customer details or secret keys into a public website.

panel.rule: Check the unit of every money field before you trust a total.

say: To remember. The URL carries the question, and JSON carries the answer. Never blindly resend a POST. Read the first digit of the status code. Count arrays from 0, and divide kobo by 100.

panel.heading: Remember
items: The URL carries the question, JSON the answer
Never blindly resend a POST
2xx success, 4xx your side, 5xx their side
Arrays start at 0; divide kobo by 100
